messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
messages.body_plain:
Hi Frank,

I just wrote a simple 'expander' in knitr as knit_expand() (currently
on Github), which should achieve the same goal as pyexpander in your
case; see https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/075-knit-expand.Rnw
for one example.

Your template would be like this:

-----------

{{
v0=paste0(v,"0") # create new variable with 0 appended
v26=paste0(v,"26")
v52=paste0(v,"52")
oth10=paste0(oth1,"0")
oth20=paste0(oth2,"0")
oth30=paste0(oth3,"0")
vupper=Hmisc::capitalize(v)     # capitalize first letters
}}

\section{Analysis of {{vupper}} Bone Mineral Density}
\subsection{26w BMD and Baseline Predictors}

In this section I model 26w interpolated BMD using baseline BMD (all
four measures, not just the target measure), baseline weight, age,
sex, race, $t$-score stratum, and treatment.  I first fit a saturated
model with respect to all of the continuous predictors, using
restricted cubic splines with 5 knots, then potentially use partial
$\chi^2$ (blinded to nonlinearity components) to reassign degrees
of freedom.

<<{{v}}-sat26,results="asis">>=
f <- ols({{v26}} ~ sex*rcs({{v0}},5) + rcs({{oth10}},5) + rcs({{oth20}},5) +
         rcs({{oth30}},5) + sex*rcs(wt0,5) + trtp + rcs(age,5) + race + sex +

         blppar + bltscgrp, data=d)
print(f, coefs=FALSE, latex=TRUE)
lan(f)
@

The global test for nonlinearity is nowhere close to being significant, so
all nonlinear effects will be dropped.

-----------

and you can expand the template by:

knit_expand("repbmd.pye", v="hip", oth1="lumbar", oth2="femur", oth3="forearm")

Actually you can vectorize the whole job by mapply():

mapply(knit_expand, file="repbmd.pye", v=c("hip", "lumbar", "femur",
"forearm"), oth1=c("lumbar", "hip", "hip", "hip"), oth2=c("femur",
"femur", "lumbar", "lumbar"), oth3=c("forearm", "forearm", "forearm",
"femur"))

This gives you the Rnw source, which is ready to be passed to knit().

I used {{}} as the tag instead of $() to avoid the awkward LaTeX math
delimiter problem, so you do not need to escape $.

Regards,
Yihui
--

This is wonderful Yihui.  Thank you for implementing this!  I really like the {{}} delimiters.  We may want to standardize on a suffix for files to be macro-expanded along the lines of .Rnwe .

pyexpander has other capabilities related to conditional text generation.  This would not be hard to do within LaTeX using \ifnum, but it would be better to have knitr not even "see" certain mixtures of LaTeX and <<>>= code chunks.  Do you think knit_expand could be expanded in that direction?  E.g.:

{{if {[v}]!=hip & \Sexpr{previous.result==3}}
.... LaTeX stuff ....
<<>>=
any number of code chunks
@
... more LaTeX text ...
{{end if}}

Thanks!
Frank

messages.body_plain:
Perhaps the conditional generation can be achieved in pure R:

{{
if (v!="hip" && previous.result==3) "

.... LaTeX stuff ....
<<>>=
any number of code chunks
@
... more LaTeX text ...
"
}}

i.e. quote the text and they will appear when the condition is TRUE.

tpl = 'an analysis
{{
if (v!="hip" && previous.result==3) "
some text
<<>>=
rnorm(5)
@
more text
"
}}
conclusions'

previous.result=1
knit_expand(text = tpl, v='hip')

previous.result=3
knit_expand(text = tpl, v='hi')

If you feel the "" syntax is awkward, you can put that part in a file,
and use `{{ if (...) readLines('template.txt') }}` instead.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.body_plain:
I guess the triple quote is not really necessary; at the moment I'm
thinking of removing the restriction on the code in {{}} so that we
can write incomplete expressions there, e.g.

{{ if (TRUE) { }}
  text for true
{{ } else { }}
  text for false
{{ } }}

{{ for (i in 1:10) { }}
  text
{{ } }}

Actually this is just re-inventing the wheel of brew, but I think the
implementation will be cleaner.

In theory this will also affect the capability of \Sexpr{} and inline
R expressions in other document formats, e.g.

`r if (TRUE) {`
  text
`r }`

But due to the poor choice of the delimiter \Sexpr{}, its curly braces
will restrict its power; "\Sexpr{ if (TRUE) { } text \Sexpr{ } }" will
not work.

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Long commands not broken properly (Overfull \hbox)
messages.body_plain:
If you do not like the automatic formatting, you can turn it off by
tidy=FALSE, and format your code by hand:

<<Test, tidy=FALSE>>=
TestObj1 <- data.frame(Name = factor(c("B", "C", "A")), Bla = rnorm(3))
TestObj2 <- data.frame(Name = factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 3)),
Bla = rnorm(9))
TestObj1 <- TestObj1[unlist(lapply(levels(TestObj2$Name),
   function(i) which(as.character(TestObj1$Name) == i))), ]
@

http://yihui.name/knitr/options

Regards,
Yihui

It may sound like an easy problem, but actually it requires an update

-- perhaps start from these files:

./src/main/names.c://{"deparseRd", 	do_deparseRd, 	0, 	11,
	2,	{PP_FUNCALL, PREC_FN, 	0}},

"do_deparse" and "deparse1"

op, SEXP args, SEXP rho)
./src/include/Internal.h:SEXP do_deparse(SEXP, SEXP, SEXP, SEXP);
./src/library/tools/src/gramRd.y:/* "do_deparseRd"
./src/library/tools/src/gramRd.c:/* "do_deparseRd"
./src/gnuwin32/Rdll.hide: do_deparse

But I would argue that whenever you see three braces in one place or a
line of more than 80 characters, you probably need to reconsider how
to organize your code. In your case, adding {} to your function will
help a lot.

TestObj1 <- TestObj1[unlist(lapply(levels(TestObj2$Name), function(i) {
  which(as.character(TestObj1$Name) == i)
})), ]

https://github.com/hadley/devtools/wiki/Style

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] long chunk output lines truncated in markdown -> pdf document
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] long chunk output lines truncated in markdown -> pdf document
messages.body_plain:
This is a such frequently asked question...

The reason is that the output is written in the verbatim environment,
so there is no way to break or wrap it, unless you modify the output
or the environment. In your case, it is harder to modify the
environment, so perhaps you should modify the output.

I have cooked up one example here:

https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/077-wrap-output.Rmd
https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/077-wrap-output.md

In RStudio you can see the line wrapped because the <pre> tag was
defined in CSS to wrap the lines:

pre {
   margin-top: 0;
   max-width: 95%;
   border: 1px solid #ccc;
   white-space: pre-wrap;
}

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.body_plain:
Sorry I should be more careful explaining the scope of opts_chunk and
knit_hooks: normally they will be restored after knit() quits, so
whatever options/hooks modified **inside** an Rnw document will only
stay inside that document.

1. get a copy of current options/hooks
2. run knit() # options/hooks may be changed inside the document
3. restore options/hooks to the values in 1

So if you have modified hooks before knit(), these hooks will still be
there after knit().

According to http://biostat.mc.vanderbilt.edu/wiki/Main/KnitrHowto,
the setup code is sourced inside an Rnw document, so all changes will
only stay inside that document. To make them persistent to the whole R
session, source() has to be done outside.

For messages.txt, yes it is under the current working directory. BTW,
if you want knitr to come to a full stop when error occurs, you can
set opts_knit$set(stop_on_error = 2). I think this is more appropriate
for production use, otherwise it is not straightforward to notice
errors.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Re: Recommended approach for repetitive sections; wish list item
messages.body_plain:
R has had dedicated templating libraries like brew and whisker. Brew, in particular allows one to harness the full capabilities of R while working on repetitive documentation. Here is a solution that combines brew and knitr to generate reproducible reports with repetitive content. The basic idea is as follows.

1. Create a template for the document (use Rnwe as extension)
2. Preprocess the template using brew to generate Rnw
3. Knit the Rnw file to generate the final report.

Steps (2) and (3) can be combined into a single function as shown below.

brew_knit <- function(template, ...){
  input = gsub(".Rnwe", ".Rnw", template)
  brew(template, input)
  knit(input, ...)
}

Here is a gist that shows the Rnwe template and the resulting Rnw file.

https://gist.github.com/4565745

Brew is very simple to use and has some very clever features that allow meta templates as well. Here is a great blog post that illustrates the power of brew

http://learnr.wordpress.com/2009/09/09/brew-creating-repetitive-reports/
